questions.stem: A white solid melts sharply at 122 °C, which is the recorded melting point of pure benzoic acid. This observation suggests that the sample is
options: a mixture of benzoic acid and common salt
benzoic acid containing water of crystallisation
an impure sample that decomposes on heating
questions.explanation: A pure substance melts sharply at a fixed temperature equal to its known melting point; impurities lower the melting point and spread it over a range.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most reliable way to check the purity of a sample of ethanol?
options: Checking that it mixes completely with water
Finding out whether it boils sharply at its known boiling point
Checking that it burns with a blue flame
questions.explanation: Constant, sharp boiling at the known temperature is a criterion of purity. Colour, miscibility and the type of flame do not show whether impurities are present.

questions.stem: Which of these is a pure substance?
questions.explanation: Distilled water contains only water molecules. Sea water, air and palm wine are all mixtures.

questions.stem: A sample of naphthalene starts to melt at 74 °C and is completely molten at 77 °C. Pure naphthalene melts at 80 °C. The most likely conclusion is that the sample
options: contains impurities, which lower its melting point and spread it over a range
is pure, because it melted below 80 °C
contains impurities, which raise its melting point
questions.explanation: Impurities lower the melting point and make melting take place over a range of temperatures instead of at one sharp temperature.

questions.stem: Paper chromatography of a black ink gives three separate coloured spots. This shows that the ink
options: is a pure compound made of three elements
is a mixture of at least three coloured substances
questions.explanation: Each spot is a separate component that moves at its own rate, so the ink must be a mixture.

questions.stem: Dissolving common salt in pure water will
options: raise its boiling point and lower its freezing point
lower its boiling point and raise its freezing point
raise both its boiling point and its freezing point
questions.explanation: A dissolved non-volatile solute raises the boiling point and lowers the freezing point of the solvent.

questions.stem: Water boils at a lower temperature on a high plateau than at sea level because
options: the air there contains less oxygen
the water there contains more dissolved impurities
heat is lost more slowly at high altitude
the atmospheric pressure is lower there, so the vapour pressure of water equals it at a lower temperature
questions.explanation: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. Lower atmospheric pressure means this happens at a lower temperature.

questions.stem: A liquid boils when
options: all its molecules have the same kinetic energy
its saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure
its temperature reaches 100 °C, whatever the pressure
questions.explanation: Boiling happens when the saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure. The boiling point therefore depends on the pressure.

questions.stem: A substance X melts at -7 °C and boils at 59 °C. At 25 °C and 1 atm, X is
options: a solid in equilibrium with its vapour
questions.explanation: 25 °C is above the melting point and below the boiling point, so X is a liquid.

questions.stem: While a pure solid is melting at its melting point, its temperature stays constant because
options: the heat absorbed is used to overcome the forces between its particles
it gives out latent heat to the surroundings
questions.explanation: Latent heat of fusion breaks the forces holding particles in the lattice, so the temperature does not rise until melting is complete.

questions.stem: Which of these substances is a compound?
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is two elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio. Brass and air are mixtures, and sulphur is an element.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a property of a mixture but NOT of a compound?
options: It has a fixed composition by mass
A definite energy change occurs when it is formed
Its components can be present in any proportion
Its properties are completely different from those of its constituents
questions.explanation: The composition of a mixture can vary. A compound has a fixed composition, a definite heat of formation and new properties.

questions.stem: Iron filings and powdered sulphur are mixed together but not heated. Which observation shows that the product is still a mixture and not iron(II) sulphide?
options: It contains both iron and sulphur
A magnet can draw out the iron from it
It is heavier than the sulphur alone
questions.explanation: In a mixture each component keeps its own properties, so the iron is still magnetic. In iron(II) sulphide the iron cannot be removed with a magnet.

questions.stem: Which of these substances is an element?
questions.explanation: Graphite is pure carbon, which is an element. Steam (H2O), limestone (CaCO3) and sand (mainly SiO2) are compounds.

questions.stem: Which of these substances is a mixture?
questions.explanation: Petrol is a mixture of many hydrocarbons. The other three are single compounds.

questions.stem: Air is classed as a mixture rather than a compound because
options: it is made up of elements only
its composition varies from place to place and its components can be separated by physical means
it can be liquefied by cooling and compression
questions.explanation: A compound has a fixed composition and can only be split up chemically. The composition of air varies, and fractional distillation separates its components.

questions.stem: Which of these everyday changes is a chemical change?
options: Rusting of an iron roofing sheet
Evaporation of water from a puddle
questions.explanation: Rusting forms a new substance, hydrated iron(III) oxide. The other changes form no new substance.

questions.stem: Which of these processes is only a physical change?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is only a change of state. No new substance is formed.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of a chemical change?
options: The total mass of the substances changes
A new substance is formed and the change is not easily reversed
The change can always be reversed by cooling
questions.explanation: Chemical changes produce new substances, usually involve a noticeable energy change and are not easily reversed. Mass is always conserved.

questions.stem: Blue hydrated copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) turns white on heating. When water is added to the white solid, it turns blue again and heat is given out. This change is best described as
options: a physical change, because it can be reversed
a chemical change, because a new substance forms with a definite energy change
questions.explanation: Water of crystallisation is chemically bound. Removing it and adding it back makes different substances, with heat absorbed and then released, so the change is chemical even though it can be reversed.

questions.stem: Which of the following processes involves a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Heat permanently changes (denatures) the proteins in an egg, forming new substances.

questions.stem: The best method of obtaining pure water from sea water is
questions.explanation: Distillation boils off the water and condenses it, leaving the dissolved salts behind. Filtration cannot remove dissolved solids.

questions.stem: A mixture of ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) and water (b.p. 100 °C) is best separated by
questions.explanation: The two liquids mix completely and have fairly close boiling points, so fractional distillation is needed.

questions.stem: Kerosene and water, which do not mix, can be separated using
questions.explanation: Immiscible liquids form two layers, and the lower layer can be run off through a separating funnel.

questions.stem: A mixture of sand, iodine and common salt is best separated by
options: heating to sublime the iodine, then adding water, filtering and evaporating the filtrate
adding water, filtering, then subliming the filtrate
fractional distillation of the whole mixture
questions.explanation: Iodine sublimes. Salt dissolves in water but sand does not, so filtration removes the sand and evaporation recovers the salt.

questions.stem: Which method can separate the coloured pigments in an extract of green leaves?
questions.explanation: The pigments move up the paper at different rates and separate into bands.

questions.stem: Chromatography works because the components of a mixture
options: move at different rates, because they are attracted differently to the stationary and mobile phases
questions.explanation: Separation depends on how strongly each component is held by the stationary phase compared with how well it dissolves in the moving solvent.

questions.stem: Which of these substances can be separated from common salt by sublimation?
questions.explanation: Ammonium chloride sublimes on heating. The others do not.

questions.stem: Copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) crystals are obtained from solution by crystallisation, not by evaporating to dryness, because evaporating to dryness would
options: drive off the water of crystallisation and give a powder
leave the solvent behind with the crystals
convert the salt into copper metal
questions.explanation: Strong heating removes the water of crystallisation. Cooling a saturated solution gives hydrated crystals.

questions.stem: Oxygen and nitrogen are obtained commercially from air by
questions.explanation: Air is liquefied and then fractionally distilled, because nitrogen and oxygen have different boiling points.

questions.stem: In the fractional distillation of liquid air, nitrogen (b.p. -196 °C) distils off before oxygen (b.p. -183 °C) because nitrogen
questions.explanation: The component with the lower boiling point vaporises first. -196 °C is lower than -183 °C.

questions.stem: Two soluble salts in a mixture have solubilities that change by very different amounts with temperature. They are best separated by
questions.explanation: When a hot saturated solution cools, the salt whose solubility falls most sharply crystallises out first.

questions.stem: Which method is used to remove insoluble solid particles from a liquid?
questions.explanation: The filter paper holds back the insoluble particles (the residue) and lets the liquid (the filtrate) through.

questions.stem: A centrifuge separates the components of a suspension such as blood because the components differ in
questions.explanation: Spinning makes the denser particles settle to the bottom faster.

questions.stem: In a paper chromatography experiment the solvent front travelled 10.0 cm and a dye spot travelled 4.5 cm from the baseline. What is the Rf value of the dye?
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent = 4.5/10.0 = 0.45. Rf values are always less than 1.

questions.stem: Which pair of substances can be separated using a magnet?
questions.explanation: Iron is magnetic and sulphur is not. Copper and zinc are not attracted to a magnet.

questions.stem: The law stating that matter is neither created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction is the law of
questions.explanation: The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.

questions.stem: Samples of copper(II) oxide made by two different methods were each found to contain 79.9% copper by mass. This illustrates the law of
questions.explanation: A given compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass, however it is made.

questions.stem: Carbon forms the oxides CO and CO2. The masses of oxygen that combine with a fixed mass of carbon in them are in the ratio 1:2. This illustrates the law of
questions.explanation: When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.

questions.stem: How many moles are present in 4.9 g of tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, H2SO4? (H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of H2SO4 = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98 g/mol, so the number of moles = 4.9/98 = 0.05 mol.

questions.stem: What is the relative molecular mass of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV), CaCO3? (C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)
A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
A hydrocarbon contains 85.7% carbon by mass and has a vapour density of 28. What is its molecular formula? (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.explanation: C:H = 85.7/12 : 14.3/1 = 7.14 : 14.3 = 1:2, so the empirical formula is CH2 (14). Mr = 2 x 28 = 56, and 56/14 = 4, giving C4H8.

questions.stem: What mass of calcium oxide is formed when 25.0 g of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) is heated until it decomposes completely? CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: 100 g of CaCO3 gives 56 g of CaO, so 25.0 g gives 25 x 56/100 = 14.0 g. 11.0 g is the mass of CO2 given off.

questions.stem: How many molecules are there in 0.25 mol of carbon(IV) oxide? (Avogadro constant = 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1)
questions.explanation: Number of molecules = moles x Avogadro constant = 0.25 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.505 x 10^23.

questions.stem: How many atoms are there in 3.2 g of oxygen gas, O2? (O = 16, Avogadro constant = 6.0 x 10^23 mol^-1)
questions.explanation: 3.2 g / 32 g/mol = 0.1 mol of O2 molecules. Each molecule has 2 atoms, so there are 0.2 mol of atoms = 0.2 x 6.0 x 10^23 = 1.2 x 10^23 atoms.

questions.stem: What volume of oxygen, measured at s.t.p., is needed to burn 4.0 g of methane completely? CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O (C = 12, H = 1; molar volume of a gas at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^3)
When the equation xAl + yO2 -> zAl2O3 is balanced, the values of x, y and z are
questions.explanation: 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3: there are 4 Al and 6 O atoms on each side.

questions.stem: The correct formula of aluminium tetraoxosulphate(VI) is
questions.explanation: Al3+ and SO4 2- combine in the ratio 2:3 so that the charges balance: 2(+3) + 3(-2) = 0.

questions.stem: When 5.0 g of hydrated sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na2CO3.xH2O, was heated to constant mass, 1.85 g of the anhydrous salt remained. What is the value of x? (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1)
What is the percentage by mass of nitrogen in ammonium trioxonitrate(V), NH4NO3? (N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Mr = 80 and the mass of nitrogen is 2 x 14 = 28, so the percentage is 28/80 x 100 = 35%. 17.5% comes from counting only one N atom.

questions.stem: What is the valency of sulphur in hydrogen sulphide, H2S?
questions.explanation: One sulphur atom combines with two hydrogen atoms, which each have valency 1, so sulphur has valency 2 here.

questions.stem: How many moles of hydrochloric acid are needed to react completely with 0.2 mol of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV)? CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2
questions.explanation: The mole ratio CaCO3 : HCl is 1 : 2, so 0.2 mol of CaCO3 needs 0.4 mol of HCl.

questions.stem: 2.4 g of magnesium is heated in a vessel containing 3.2 g of oxygen gas. What mass of magnesium oxide is formed? 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO (Mg = 24, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Mg = 0.1 mol and O2 = 0.1 mol. 0.1 mol of Mg needs only 0.05 mol of O2, so Mg is the limiting reactant and forms 0.1 mol of MgO = 4.0 g. 5.6 g wrongly assumes all the oxygen reacts.

questions.stem: An oxide of copper contains 3.175 g of copper combined with 0.80 g of oxygen. What is its empirical formula? (Cu = 63.5, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Cu = 3.175/63.5 = 0.05 mol and O = 0.80/16 = 0.05 mol. The ratio is 1:1, so the formula is CuO.

questions.stem: 0.48 g of a metal M (relative atomic mass 24) reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid and gives 448 cm^3 of hydrogen measured at s.t.p. What is the formula of the chloride of M? (Molar volume at s.t.p. = 22 400 cm^3)
questions.explanation: M = 0.48/24 = 0.02 mol and H2 = 448/22400 = 0.02 mol. One mole of M releases one mole of H2, so M loses 2 electrons and forms M2+, giving MCl2.

questions.stem: The relative atomic masses of elements are now measured relative to
options: the mass of a hydrogen atom
one-sixteenth of the mass of an oxygen atom
one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
questions.explanation: The modern scale defines the mass of one atom of carbon-12 as exactly 12 units.

questions.stem: According to the kinetic theory, the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas is directly proportional to its
questions.explanation: Average kinetic energy depends only on the absolute (kelvin) temperature.

questions.stem: Which assumption of the kinetic theory of gases is NOT valid for a real gas at very high pressure?
options: The molecules are in constant random motion
The molecules move in straight lines between collisions
The pressure is caused by molecules hitting the walls of the container
The volume of the gas molecules themselves is negligible compared with the volume of the container
questions.explanation: At high pressure the molecules are crowded together, so their own volume is no longer negligible.

questions.stem: The random movement of pollen grains seen under a microscope when they are suspended in water is evidence that
options: water molecules are in constant random motion
questions.explanation: Brownian motion is caused by uneven bombardment of the grains by moving water molecules.

questions.stem: Diffusion takes place fastest in
questions.explanation: Gas particles are far apart and move fastest, so they mix most quickly.

questions.stem: When a gas is heated in a closed, rigid container, its pressure rises because the molecules
options: move faster and hit the walls more often and with greater force
questions.explanation: A higher temperature raises the average speed of the molecules, so collisions with the walls are more frequent and more forceful.

questions.stem: Which change of state involves particles passing directly from the solid state to the gaseous state?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is a direct change from solid to gas, as when iodine or ammonium chloride is heated.

questions.stem: Evaporation cools the liquid that is left behind because
options: the liquid absorbs heat from its own vapour
evaporation only happens at the boiling point
the molecules with the highest kinetic energy escape, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules falls
questions.explanation: Only the fastest molecules can escape from the surface. Their loss lowers the average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, of the liquid left behind.

questions.stem: The particles in a solid
options: move about randomly through the whole container
are far apart with almost no forces between them
questions.explanation: Strong forces hold the particles of a solid in fixed positions, so they can only vibrate.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 300 cm^3 at a pressure of 1.0 atm. If the temperature stays the same, what will its volume be at 1.5 atm?
questions.explanation: By Boyle's law, P1V1 = P2V2, so V2 = (1.0 x 300)/1.5 = 200 cm^3.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 250 cm^3 at 27 °C. What is its volume at 87 °C if the pressure stays constant?
questions.explanation: By Charles' law the temperatures must be in kelvin: V2 = 250 x 360/300 = 300 cm^3. 806 cm^3 comes from wrongly using degrees Celsius.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 400 cm^3 at 27 °C and 760 mmHg. What is its volume at s.t.p.?
questions.explanation: The pressure does not change, so V2 = 400 x 273/300 = 364 cm^3.

questions.stem: A fixed mass of gas occupies 6.0 dm^3 at 2.0 atm and 127 °C. What is its volume at 1.0 atm and 27 °C?
Under the same conditions, how does the rate of diffusion of hydrogen compare with that of oxygen? (H = 1, O = 16)
questions.explanation: By Graham's law, rate(H2)/rate(O2) = sqrt(32/2) = sqrt(16) = 4.

questions.stem: A gas X diffuses at half the rate of methane, CH4, under the same conditions. What is the relative molecular mass of X? (C = 12, H = 1)
questions.explanation: rate(X)/rate(CH4) = sqrt(16/Mx) = 1/2, so 16/Mx = 1/4 and Mx = 64.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.2 mol of nitrogen and 0.3 mol of oxygen at a total pressure of 100 kPa. What is the partial pressure of the oxygen?
questions.explanation: By Dalton's law, partial pressure = mole fraction x total pressure = (0.3/0.5) x 100 = 60 kPa.

questions.stem: Hydrogen collected over water at 25 °C has a total pressure of 750 mmHg. The saturated vapour pressure of water at 25 °C is 24 mmHg. What is the pressure of the dry hydrogen?
questions.explanation: Total pressure = p(H2) + p(water vapour), so p(H2) = 750 - 24 = 726 mmHg.

questions.stem: Boyle's law states that, at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is
options: directly proportional to its absolute temperature
questions.explanation: PV = constant at constant temperature, so doubling the pressure halves the volume.

questions.stem: Standard temperature and pressure (s.t.p.) means
questions.explanation: s.t.p. is 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atmosphere (760 mmHg).

questions.stem: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of
questions.explanation: The law refers to molecules. For example, O2 and O3 samples of the same volume have the same number of molecules but different numbers of atoms.

questions.stem: 30 cm^3 of hydrogen reacts completely with excess nitrogen: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. What volume of ammonia is formed, all volumes being measured under the same conditions?
questions.explanation: By Gay-Lussac's law the volume ratio H2 : NH3 is 3 : 2, so 30 cm^3 of H2 gives 20 cm^3 of NH3.

questions.stem: 40 cm^3 of carbon(II) oxide is sparked with 60 cm^3 of oxygen: 2CO + O2 -> 2CO2. What is the total volume of gas left at the original temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: 40 cm^3 of CO uses 20 cm^3 of O2 and forms 40 cm^3 of CO2. 40 cm^3 of O2 is left over, so the total is 40 + 40 = 80 cm^3.

questions.stem: Using PV = nRT, what volume does 0.5 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 300 K and 1.0 x 10^5 Pa? (R = 8.31 J mol^-1 K^-1)
What is the mass of 5.6 dm^3 of carbon(IV) oxide at s.t.p.? (C = 12, O = 16; molar volume at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^3)
A gas has a density of 1.25 g dm^-3 at s.t.p. What is its relative molecular mass? (Molar volume at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^3)
questions.explanation: Molar mass = density x molar volume = 1.25 x 22.4 = 28 g/mol.

questions.stem: Real gases come closest to ideal behaviour at
questions.explanation: At low pressure the molecules are far apart, and at high temperature they move fast, so their own volume and the attractions between them matter least.

questions.stem: For a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, a graph of volume against absolute temperature is
options: a straight line through the origin
a straight line parallel to the temperature axis
a curve that rises steeply and then levels off
questions.explanation: Charles' law: V is directly proportional to T in kelvin, so the graph is a straight line through the origin.

questions.stem: 20 cm^3 of hydrogen reacts with excess chlorine. What volume of hydrogen chloride is formed at the same temperature and pressure? H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl
questions.explanation: The volume ratio H2 : HCl is 1 : 2, so 20 cm^3 of H2 gives 40 cm^3 of HCl.

questions.stem: A gas cylinder holds oxygen at 27 °C and 3.0 atm. If the temperature rises to 77 °C and the volume stays the same, what is the new pressure?
questions.explanation: At constant volume P/T is constant: P2 = 3.0 x 350/300 = 3.5 atm. 8.6 atm comes from using degrees Celsius.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: An atom has mass number 31 and atomic number 15. How many neutrons does it contain?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 31 - 15 = 16.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: Which particle has almost no mass and a charge of -1?
questions.explanation: The mass of an electron is about 1/1840 of the mass of a proton, and it carries one unit of negative charge.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment showed that
options: electrons move in fixed energy levels
atoms are solid spheres that cannot be divided
an atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, but a few were deflected sharply. This shows a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus. Neutrons were discovered later, by Chadwick.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: Isotopes of an element have the same
options: number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
mass number but different atomic numbers
number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number (number of protons) but different mass numbers, because the number of neutrons differs.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: Chlorine is made up of 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. What is its relative atomic mass?

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: An element X has two isotopes, X-63 and X-65, and its relative atomic mass is 63.6. What percentage of X atoms are X-65?
questions.explanation: Let the fraction of X-65 be p. Then 63(1 - p) + 65p = 63.6, so 2p = 0.6 and p = 0.30, which is 30%.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: What is the electronic configuration of potassium, atomic number 19?
questions.explanation: The 4s orbital is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first. A p sub-level holds at most 6 electrons.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: How many unpaired electrons does a nitrogen atom (atomic number 7) have in its ground state?
questions.explanation: The configuration is 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3. By Hund's rule the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals, so all three are unpaired.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: Which of these ions has the same electronic configuration as neon?
questions.explanation: Na+ has 10 electrons (2,8), the same as neon. K+, Cl- and Ca2+ each have 18 electrons, like argon.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons that a d sub-level can hold?
questions.explanation: A d sub-level has 5 orbitals, each holding 2 electrons, so it holds 10 electrons.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: The rule stating that electrons occupy orbitals of equal energy singly, with parallel spins, before any pairing takes place is
questions.explanation: Hund's rule deals with filling degenerate orbitals. Pauli's principle limits an orbital to two electrons of opposite spin, and the Aufbau principle orders filling by energy.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: How many electrons are there in the ion 26Fe3+?
questions.explanation: Iron has 26 electrons. Losing three to form Fe3+ leaves 26 - 3 = 23.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: Which quantum number describes the shape of an orbital?
questions.explanation: l decides whether an orbital is s, p, d or f, and so its shape. n gives the energy level, and m gives the orientation.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: The charge on the nucleus of an atom depends on the number of
questions.explanation: Protons are the only charged particles in the nucleus.

questions.topic: Atoms, molecules and ions; atomic structure
questions.stem: Cathode rays are made up of streams of
questions.explanation: Cathode rays are bent towards a positive plate, which shows they carry negative charge. They are electrons.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same
questions.explanation: Group number is linked to the number of outer-shell electrons, and this gives the elements of a group similar chemical properties.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally
options: increases, because more electrons are added
decreases, because nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell
decreases, because electron shells are lost
questions.explanation: The increasing nuclear charge pulls the electrons in the same shell closer to the nucleus.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: Which of these elements has the highest first ionisation energy?
questions.explanation: Ionisation energy is highest at the top right of the periodic table. Helium's two electrons are close to the nucleus and form a full shell.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: An element has the electronic configuration 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^4. Where is it in the periodic table?
questions.explanation: There are 6 valence electrons in the third shell (3s^2 3p^4), so it is in Group 6 (16) and Period 3. It is sulphur.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: Which element is the most electronegative?
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element of all. It is small and has a high effective nuclear charge.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: The reactivity of Group 1 metals increases down the group because
options: the nuclear charge decreases down the group
the atoms become smaller down the group
the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost
questions.explanation: Extra shells and shielding make the single valence electron easier to remove, so the metal reacts more readily.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: Which of these trends is correct going down Group 7 (the halogens)?
options: The elements become paler in colour
questions.explanation: Going down the group the atoms get larger, gain electrons less easily, and their colour gets darker (from pale yellow fluorine to dark iodine).

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: The noble gases are unreactive because
options: they are gases at room temperature
their outermost electron shells are full
they have high relative atomic masses
questions.explanation: A full outer shell (a stable octet, or duplet for helium) gives them little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: Which of these is a transition element?
questions.explanation: Chromium is a d-block element in the first transition series. The other three are main-group elements.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: An element Z has atomic number 12. Which ion is it most likely to form?
questions.explanation: The configuration is 2,8,2. Z loses its two outer electrons to reach the stable 2,8 arrangement.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: Across Period 3 from sodium to chlorine, the oxides of the elements change from
questions.explanation: Na2O and MgO are basic, Al2O3 is amphoteric, and the oxides of Si, P, S and Cl are acidic, as metallic character decreases across the period.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: The modern periodic law states that the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their
questions.explanation: Moseley showed that ordering by atomic number, not atomic mass, gives the correct periodic pattern.

questions.topic: Periodic table and periodicity of elements
questions.stem: Which of these Period 3 elements has the largest atomic radius?
questions.explanation: Atomic radius decreases across a period, so sodium, at the start of the period, has the largest atoms.

questions.stem: What type of bonding is present in sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming Na+ and Cl- ions, which are held together by electrostatic attraction.

questions.stem: Which of these compounds contains a dative (coordinate) covalent bond?
questions.explanation: In NH4+ the nitrogen's lone pair is donated to an H+ ion, forming a dative bond.

questions.stem: Hydrogen bonding explains why water
options: has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulphide
is made up of hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 ratio
questions.explanation: The strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules need more energy to break than the weak forces between H2S molecules.

questions.stem: Which of these substances conducts electricity when molten but not when solid?
questions.explanation: In solid NaCl the ions are fixed in place. When it melts they become free to move and carry current. Copper and graphite conduct when solid, and sugar never conducts.

questions.stem: Metallic bonding is best described as
options: the sharing of electron pairs between neighbouring metal atoms only
positive metal ions held together by a sea of delocalised electrons
the transfer of electrons from one metal atom to another
attraction between oppositely charged metal ions
questions.explanation: The valence electrons are free to move through the lattice. This explains why metals conduct electricity and can be hammered into shape.

questions.stem: How many pairs of electrons are shared between the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule, N2?
questions.explanation: Each N atom needs 3 more electrons to complete its octet, so the atoms share three pairs, forming a triple bond.

questions.stem: Which molecule is non-polar even though its bonds are polar?
questions.explanation: CO2 is linear, so the two C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel out.

questions.stem: Simple covalent compounds generally
options: have low melting and boiling points
questions.explanation: Only weak intermolecular forces hold their molecules together, so little energy is needed to melt or boil them.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity because
options: each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that can move between the layers
each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Each carbon in graphite forms only three bonds. The fourth electron is delocalised along the layers and carries the current.

questions.stem: The boiling points of the noble gases increase down the group because
options: the atoms form covalent bonds with each other
ionisation energy increases down the group
larger atoms have more electrons, so the van der Waals forces between them are stronger
the atoms become smaller down the group
questions.explanation: More electrons can be distorted more easily, giving stronger temporary dipole attractions, so more energy is needed to separate the atoms.

questions.stem: An element X (atomic number 11) combines with an element Y (atomic number 17). What is the bonding in the compound, and what is its formula?
questions.explanation: X (2,8,1) loses one electron and Y (2,8,7) gains one, so they form the ionic compound XY (sodium chloride).

questions.stem: Diamond is very hard because
options: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network
its layers slide over one another
it is made up of small separate molecules
questions.explanation: Diamond is a giant covalent structure. Strong bonds in every direction make it very hard.

questions.stem: What is the shape of a methane molecule?
questions.explanation: Four bonding pairs around the carbon atom repel one another equally, giving a tetrahedron with bond angles of 109.5°.

questions.stem: What is the approximate H-O-H bond angle in a water molecule?
questions.explanation: The two lone pairs on oxygen squeeze the bonding pairs closer together, reducing the angle below the tetrahedral 109.5°.

questions.stem: What is the shape of an ammonia molecule?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair. The lone pair pushes the three N-H bonds into a pyramid.

questions.stem: What is the shape of a boron trifluoride (BF3) molecule?
questions.explanation: Boron has three bonding pairs and no lone pair, so the bonds lie in one plane at 120° to each other.

questions.stem: What is the shape of a carbon(IV) oxide molecule?
questions.explanation: The carbon atom has two double bonds and no lone pairs, so the bonds point in opposite directions (180°).

questions.stem: The bond angle in ammonia (about 107°) is smaller than the tetrahedral angle of 109.5° because
options: nitrogen is less electronegative than hydrogen
the lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly than the bonding pairs repel each other
the nitrogen atom is sp hybridised
questions.explanation: Lone pair-bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair-bond pair repulsion, so the N-H bonds are pushed slightly closer together.

questions.stem: An alpha particle is
questions.explanation: An alpha particle contains 2 protons and 2 neutrons, which is the same as a He2+ nucleus.

questions.stem: When a nucleus emits a beta particle,
options: its atomic number increases by 1 and its mass number stays the same
its atomic number decreases by 2 and its mass number decreases by 4
its atomic number and mass number both stay the same
questions.explanation: A neutron changes into a proton and an electron, and the electron is emitted. The proton count rises by one, but the total number of nucleons does not change.

questions.stem: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) emits an alpha particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the nucleus that forms?
questions.explanation: Alpha emission removes 4 from the mass number and 2 from the atomic number: 238 - 4 = 234 and 92 - 2 = 90 (thorium).

questions.stem: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 8 days. What fraction of a sample of it is left after 32 days?
questions.explanation: 32 days is 4 half-lives, so the fraction left is (1/2)^4 = 1/16.

questions.stem: A sample contains 80 g of a radioactive isotope. What mass of the isotope is left after three half-lives?
questions.explanation: The mass halves three times: 80 -> 40 -> 20 -> 10 g.

questions.stem: The activity of a radioactive source falls from 1600 counts per minute to 100 counts per minute in 20 hours. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation: 1600 -> 800 -> 400 -> 200 -> 100 is 4 half-lives, so the half-life is 20/4 = 5 hours.

questions.stem: Which type of radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves and need thick lead or concrete to stop them. A sheet of paper stops alpha particles.

questions.stem: Nuclear fission is
options: the joining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
the splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, with the release of a large amount of energy
the emission of an electron from the nucleus
the burning of uranium in oxygen
questions.explanation: In fission a heavy nucleus such as U-235 absorbs a neutron and splits. The joining of light nuclei is fusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct use of a radioisotope?
options: Cobalt-60 is used in the treatment of cancer
Uranium-235 is used as a fertiliser
Carbon-12 is used to find the age of ancient wood
Hydrogen-1 is the fuel in nuclear fission reactors
questions.explanation: Gamma rays from cobalt-60 destroy cancer cells. Carbon-14, not carbon-12, is used for dating.

questions.stem: When a nucleus emits gamma radiation,
options: neither its atomic number nor its mass number changes
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are energy with no mass and no charge. They only release excess energy from the nucleus.

questions.stem: In the nuclear reaction 14/7 N + 4/2 He -> 17/8 O + X (mass number/atomic number), what is X?
questions.explanation: Mass number: 14 + 4 = 17 + 1. Atomic number: 7 + 2 = 8 + 1. A particle with mass 1 and charge +1 is a proton.

questions.stem: Which gas makes up the largest proportion of air?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of air by volume.

questions.stem: About what percentage of air by volume is oxygen?
questions.explanation: Oxygen makes up about one-fifth (21%) of air by volume.

questions.stem: When a sample of air is passed repeatedly over heated copper, its volume falls by about one-fifth. This is because
options: the nitrogen reacts with the copper
the oxygen combines with the copper to form copper(II) oxide
the copper absorbs the water vapour
questions.explanation: Hot copper removes the oxygen as black CuO. Oxygen is about 21% (one-fifth) of air.

questions.stem: Which reagent will absorb carbon(IV) oxide from a sample of air?
questions.explanation: KOH reacts with the acidic gas CO2. Alkaline pyrogallol and heated copper remove oxygen, and concentrated H2SO4 removes water vapour.

questions.stem: About what percentage of air by volume is carbon(IV) oxide?
questions.explanation: CO2 is only a trace gas in air (about 0.03 to 0.04%). Argon makes up about 0.93%.

questions.stem: Anhydrous calcium chloride left open to the air soon becomes wet. This shows that air contains
questions.explanation: Calcium chloride takes up water vapour from the air (deliquescence).

questions.topic: Air as a mixture and uses of noble gases
questions.stem: Argon is used to fill electric light bulbs because
options: it is inert and does not react with the hot filament
it is a good conductor of electricity
it absorbs heat from the filament
questions.explanation: An unreactive gas stops the hot tungsten filament from oxidising.

questions.topic: Air as a mixture and uses of noble gases
questions.stem: Which noble gas is used in advertising signs that give a red-orange glow?
questions.explanation: Neon glows red-orange when an electric discharge passes through it.

questions.topic: Air as a mixture and uses of noble gases
questions.stem: Helium is used in weather balloons in preference to hydrogen because helium is
questions.explanation: Helium is less dense than air and, unlike hydrogen, does not burn, so it is safer.

questions.topic: Air as a mixture and uses of noble gases
questions.stem: Which observation supports the view that air is a mixture?
options: Liquid air boils over a range of temperatures instead of at a single fixed temperature
questions.explanation: A pure substance boils at a fixed temperature. Liquid air boils over a range because its components boil off separately.

questions.topic: Air as a mixture and uses of noble gases
questions.stem: Which noble gas is present in the largest amount in air?
questions.explanation: Argon makes up about 0.93% of air, far more than the other noble gases.

questions.stem: When hydrogen burns in oxygen to form water, the gases combine in the volume ratio
options: 1 volume of hydrogen to 2 volumes of oxygen
2 volumes of hydrogen to 1 volume of oxygen
1 volume of hydrogen to 1 volume of oxygen
3 volumes of hydrogen to 1 volume of oxygen
questions.explanation: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. By Gay-Lussac's law the volume ratio is the same as the mole ratio, 2:1.

questions.stem: Temporary hardness of water is caused by dissolved
questions.explanation: Ca(HCO3)2 and Mg(HCO3)2 cause temporary hardness. Sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium cause permanent hardness.

questions.stem: Temporary hardness can be removed by boiling because
options: the hydrogentrioxocarbonate(IV) decomposes and insoluble calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) is precipitated
boiling drives off the calcium ions as a gas
boiling converts calcium ions to sodium ions
questions.explanation: Ca(HCO3)2 -> CaCO3 + H2O + CO2. The calcium ions are removed as the solid (scale or fur) seen in kettles.

questions.stem: Permanent hardness of water can be removed by
questions.explanation: Na2CO3 precipitates Ca2+ and Mg2+ as insoluble carbonates. Boiling does not remove sulphates or chlorides.

questions.stem: Hard water wastes soap because
options: it dissolves the soap too quickly
calcium and magnesium ions react with soap to form an insoluble scum
it is too acidic for soap to work
questions.explanation: Soap only lathers once all the Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions have been precipitated as scum.

questions.stem: In the treatment of water for town supply, chlorine is added to
questions.explanation: Chlorination sterilises the water. Alum is used to coagulate suspended particles.

questions.stem: Alum is added to water during treatment for town supply in order to
options: coagulate fine suspended particles so that they settle
questions.explanation: Alum makes the tiny suspended particles clump together (flocculate) so that they settle in the sedimentation tanks.

questions.stem: A substance that absorbs water vapour from the air and dissolves in it to form a solution is said to be
questions.explanation: Deliquescent substances, such as CaCl2 and NaOH, absorb so much water that they dissolve. Hygroscopic substances absorb water but do not dissolve.

questions.stem: Washing soda crystals, Na2CO3.10H2O, left open to the air lose some of their water of crystallisation and become powdery. This is called
questions.explanation: Efflorescent substances give up water of crystallisation to the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Which of the following is hygroscopic?
questions.explanation: Concentrated H2SO4 absorbs water vapour from the air without forming a solid, which is why it is used as a drying agent.

questions.stem: An advantage of hard water is that it
options: supplies calcium needed for strong bones and teeth
does not form scale in kettles
questions.explanation: The dissolved calcium salts are useful in the diet. The other statements are false for hard water.

questions.stem: Oxygen dissolved in river water is important mainly because
options: aquatic organisms use it for respiration
it prevents the water from freezing
it gives the water its taste
questions.explanation: Fish and other aquatic organisms depend on dissolved oxygen for respiration.

questions.stem: Water is a good solvent for many ionic compounds because
options: it has a high boiling point
its molecules are polar and surround (hydrate) the separated ions
questions.explanation: The partial charges on water molecules attract the ions, releasing hydration energy that helps to break up the crystal lattice.

questions.stem: In the ion-exchange method of softening water, the exchanger (permutit) works by
options: replacing calcium and magnesium ions in the water with sodium ions
questions.explanation: The resin holds Na+ ions, which it swaps for Ca2+ and Mg2+ as the hard water passes through.

questions.stem: Which of these tests shows that a liquid contains water?
options: It turns white anhydrous copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) blue
questions.explanation: Anhydrous CuSO4 takes up water and turns blue. (Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride, which turns from blue to pink, also works.)

questions.stem: A solution that can dissolve no more solute at a given temperature is described as
questions.explanation: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute it can hold at that temperature, in contact with undissolved solute.

questions.stem: A supersaturated solution
options: contains less solute than a saturated solution
can dissolve more solute at the same temperature
contains more solute than it can normally hold at that temperature, and crystallises when a seed crystal is added
is a mixture of two solvents
questions.explanation: Supersaturated solutions are unstable. A seed crystal or a scratch starts crystallisation of the excess solute.

questions.stem: At 30 °C, 25 cm^3 of a saturated solution of a salt X (molar mass 80 g/mol) gave 2.0 g of dry X on evaporation. What is the solubility of X at 30 °C in mol dm^-3?
questions.explanation: Moles of X = 2.0/80 = 0.025 mol in 0.025 dm^3, so solubility = 0.025/0.025 = 1.0 mol dm^-3.

questions.stem: The solubility of a salt Y (molar mass 100 g/mol) is 2.0 mol dm^-3 at 60 °C and 0.5 mol dm^-3 at 20 °C. What mass of Y crystallises out when 500 cm^3 of saturated solution is cooled from 60 °C to 20 °C? (Ignore any change in volume.)
questions.explanation: Moles that come out of solution = (2.0 - 0.5) x 0.500 = 0.75 mol, and 0.75 x 100 = 75 g. 150 g forgets to scale to 500 cm^3.

questions.stem: For most solid solutes, solubility in water
questions.explanation: Most solubility curves of solids slope upwards. (A few salts, such as calcium hydroxide, are exceptions.)

questions.stem: Why does the solubility of oxygen in water fall when the water is warmed?
options: The dissolved gas molecules gain kinetic energy and escape from the solution
questions.explanation: Gas solubility decreases with temperature. Warm, polluted rivers therefore hold less oxygen for aquatic life.

questions.stem: Which liquid is best for removing a palm oil stain from a cloth?
questions.explanation: Oils and fats dissolve in non-polar organic solvents such as kerosene or petrol, but not in water.

questions.stem: Nail varnish (a paint-like stain) is usually removed with
questions.explanation: Propanone is an organic solvent that dissolves lacquers and paints.

questions.stem: Which of these is a colloid?
questions.explanation: Milk is an emulsion (a colloid) of fat droplets in water. Harmattan haze and muddy water are suspensions, and salt solution is a true solution.

questions.stem: Harmattan haze is an example of
questions.explanation: Harmattan haze is made of dust particles big enough to settle out of the air in time, so it is a suspension.

questions.stem: When a beam of light is passed through fog, the path of the beam becomes visible. This is because
options: the particles absorb all the light
the colloidal particles scatter the light (the Tyndall effect)
questions.explanation: Colloidal particles are large enough to scatter light, so the beam shows up.

questions.stem: A true solution differs from a suspension in that a true solution
options: does not settle on standing and passes through filter paper unchanged
leaves a residue on filter paper
questions.explanation: Solute particles in a true solution are of molecular or ionic size, so they neither settle nor are held back by a filter.

questions.stem: Which pair of substances are both colloids?
questions.explanation: Fog, emulsion paint, milk and rubber solution are colloids. Harmattan haze and muddy water are suspensions, and sea water is a true solution.

questions.stem: A gas is produced when fuel burns in a poorly ventilated room, and it combines with haemoglobin to cause suffocation. The gas is
questions.explanation: Incomplete combustion produces CO, which binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does. This is why generators should never be run indoors.

questions.stem: Acid rain is caused mainly by
options: sulphur(IV) oxide and oxides of nitrogen
questions.explanation: SO2 and NOx dissolve in rainwater to form acids such as H2SO3, H2SO4 and HNO3.

questions.stem: The depletion of the ozone layer is mainly caused by
questions.explanation: Chlorine atoms released from CFCs in the upper atmosphere break down ozone molecules.

questions.stem: Which of these pollutants is biodegradable?
questions.explanation: Micro-organisms can decompose organic waste such as vegetable peels. Plastics, glass and metal cans are not broken down by them.

questions.stem: Crude oil spilled into creeks harms aquatic life mainly because the oil
options: raises the oxygen content of the water
forms a film on the water surface that cuts down oxygen dissolving and coats the organisms
dissolves completely and poisons only the plants
questions.explanation: The surface film stops oxygen dissolving and light getting through, and it coats the gills and feathers of animals.

questions.stem: Which pollutant gas from oil refineries and decaying matter smells of rotten eggs?
questions.explanation: H2S is poisonous and has a characteristic smell of rotten eggs.

questions.stem: When untreated sewage is discharged into a river,
options: the dissolved oxygen falls as micro-organisms decompose the sewage
questions.explanation: Aerobic decomposers use up dissolved oxygen (a high biochemical oxygen demand), which can suffocate fish.

questions.stem: The enhanced greenhouse effect is caused mainly by a rise in the atmospheric concentration of
questions.explanation: CO2 from burning fossil fuels and from deforestation traps outgoing infrared radiation.

questions.stem: A catalytic converter fitted to a car exhaust reduces pollution by converting
options: carbon(II) oxide and nitrogen oxides into carbon(IV) oxide and nitrogen
questions.explanation: Platinum-group catalysts oxidise CO to CO2 and reduce NO to N2.

questions.stem: Lead compounds once added to petrol were harmful mainly because lead
options: builds up in the body and damages the nervous system
questions.explanation: Lead is a cumulative poison that is especially harmful to children's brain development.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-biodegradable pollutant?
questions.explanation: Plastics resist decomposition by micro-organisms and stay in the environment for a very long time.

questions.stem: An acid is a substance which, in aqueous solution, produces
options: hydroxonium ions (H3O+) as the only positive ions
hydroxide ions as the only negative ions
questions.explanation: In water, acids donate protons to water molecules, forming H3O+ ions.

questions.stem: In the Bronsted-Lowry theory, a base is defined as
options: a substance that produces H3O+ ions in water
a substance that donates a lone pair to a metal only
questions.explanation: Bronsted-Lowry acids donate protons (H+) and bases accept them.

questions.stem: What is the basicity of ethanoic acid, CH3COOH?
questions.explanation: Only the hydrogen of the -COOH group can be replaced, so the basicity is 1, even though the molecule has 4 hydrogen atoms.

questions.stem: What is the basicity of tetraoxophosphate(V) acid, H3PO4?
questions.explanation: Each molecule has three replaceable hydrogen atoms, so it is tribasic.

questions.stem: Sodium hydrogentetraoxosulphate(VI), NaHSO4, is an example of
questions.explanation: Only part of the replaceable hydrogen of H2SO4 has been replaced by a metal, so it is an acid salt.

questions.stem: Potash alum, K2SO4.Al2(SO4)3.24H2O, is an example of
options: a complex salt containing no water
questions.explanation: It contains two different cations (K+ and Al3+) combined with one anion, so it is a double salt.

questions.stem: Barium tetraoxosulphate(VI), an insoluble salt, is best prepared by
options: titrating an acid with an alkali
adding barium metal to the acid
questions.explanation: Mixing solutions of a soluble barium salt and a soluble sulphate precipitates BaSO4, which is then filtered, washed and dried.

questions.stem: The main acid found in oranges and lemons is
questions.explanation: Citrus fruits contain citric acid. Tartaric acid is found in grapes and ethanoic acid in vinegar.

questions.stem: Which of these oxides is amphoteric?
questions.explanation: ZnO reacts with both acids and alkalis. Na2O and CaO are basic, and SO3 is acidic.

questions.stem: A 1.0 mol dm^-3 solution of ethanoic acid conducts electricity less well than 1.0 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid because ethanoic acid
options: is only partly ionised in water
questions.explanation: A weak acid produces fewer ions in solution, so it conducts electricity poorly.

questions.stem: Which of these solutions will turn red litmus blue?
questions.explanation: Alkalis turn red litmus blue.

questions.stem: Which of the following salts is insoluble in water?
questions.explanation: Almost all sodium, potassium, ammonium and trioxonitrate(V) salts are soluble. AgCl is an insoluble chloride.

questions.stem: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a trioxocarbonate(IV), a gas is given off that turns lime water milky. The gas is
questions.explanation: Carbonate + acid -> salt + water + CO2. CO2 turns lime water milky.

questions.stem: A solution with a pH of 2 is
questions.explanation: A pH well below 7 shows a high concentration of hydrogen ions.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.001 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: HCl is fully ionised, so [H+] = 10^-3 mol dm^-3 and pH = -log(10^-3) = 3.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.01 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide solution at 25 °C?
A solution has a hydrogen ion concentration of 1.0 x 10^-5 mol dm^-3. What is its pOH at 25 °C?
The pOH of a solution is 4. What is its pH at 25 °C?
How does the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution of pH 3 compare with that of a solution of pH 5?
questions.explanation: Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so a difference of 2 units is 10^2 = 100. The lower pH has the higher [H+].

questions.stem: Which of these solutions has the highest pH?
questions.explanation: NaOH is a strong alkali (pH about 13). Pure water is 7 and the acids are below 7.

questions.stem: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: In pure water [H+] = [OH-] = 10^-7 mol dm^-3, so pH = 7.

questions.stem: What is the hydroxide ion concentration of a solution of pH 11 at 25 °C?
Unpolluted rainwater has a pH slightly below 7 because
options: dissolved carbon(IV) oxide forms trioxocarbonate(IV) acid
questions.explanation: CO2 + H2O <=> H2CO3, a weak acid, gives natural rain a pH of about 5.6.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm^3 of 0.10 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm^3 of hydrochloric acid. What is the concentration of the acid?
questions.explanation: NaOH + HCl react 1:1, so Ca x 20.0 = 0.10 x 25.0 and Ca = 0.125 mol dm^-3.

questions.stem: What volume of 0.20 mol dm^-3 tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid will exactly neutralise 30.0 cm^3 of 0.10 mol dm^-3 sodium hydroxide? H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O
questions.explanation: NaOH = 0.10 x 0.030 = 0.0030 mol, so H2SO4 needed = 0.0015 mol. Volume = 0.0015/0.20 = 0.0075 dm^3 = 7.5 cm^3. 15.0 cm^3 ignores the 1:2 ratio.

questions.stem: 2.65 g of anhydrous sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm^3. What is the concentration of the solution? (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.explanation: Molar mass of Na2CO3 = 106 g/mol. 2.65/106 = 0.025 mol in 0.250 dm^3, so the concentration is 0.025/0.250 = 0.100 mol dm^-3.

questions.stem: Which indicator is most suitable for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation: A weak acid-strong base titration has its end point in the alkaline range (about pH 8 to 10), where phenolphthalein changes colour.

questions.stem: Which indicator is most suitable for titrating hydrochloric acid with aqueous ammonia?
questions.explanation: A strong acid-weak base titration has an acidic end point (about pH 3 to 5), which methyl orange shows.

questions.stem: What mass of sodium hydroxide is needed to make 250 cm^3 of a 0.20 mol dm^-3 solution? (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
20.0 cm^3 of 0.050 mol dm^-3 tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid exactly neutralised 25.0 cm^3 of potassium hydroxide solution. What is the concentration of the KOH in g dm^-3? (K = 39, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.explanation: H2SO4 = 0.0010 mol, so KOH = 0.0020 mol in 0.025 dm^3, which is 0.080 mol dm^-3. Multiplying by 56 g/mol gives 4.48 g dm^-3.

questions.stem: Which apparatus is used to deliver accurately measured, variable volumes of acid during a titration?
questions.explanation: A burette has a tap and a graduated scale, so the volume added can be read accurately. A pipette delivers only one fixed volume.

questions.stem: Before it is used in a titration, a pipette should be rinsed with
options: the solution it is going to deliver
questions.explanation: Rinsing with the solution itself stops leftover water from diluting the measured portion.

questions.stem: An aqueous solution of sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) is alkaline because the salt
options: is formed from a strong acid and a weak base
is formed from a strong base and a weak acid, so its anion hydrolyses to give OH- ions
questions.explanation: CO3 2- + H2O <=> HCO3- + OH-. The excess OH- ions make the solution alkaline.

questions.stem: An aqueous solution of ammonium chloride is
questions.explanation: NH4Cl is the salt of a strong acid and a weak base. NH4+ gives up a proton to water, forming H3O+.

questions.stem: Which of these salts gives a neutral aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: NaCl comes from a strong acid and a strong base, so neither of its ions hydrolyses.

questions.stem: A solution of iron(III) chloride in water is acidic because
options: the hydrated Fe3+ ion reacts with water and releases H3O+ ions
chloride ions react with water to form hydroxide ions
iron is a transition metal and all its compounds are acids
questions.explanation: The small, highly charged Fe3+ ion polarises the water molecules around it so that they release protons.

questions.stem: A solution of sodium ethanoate turns red litmus blue because
options: ethanoate ions are oxidised by air
the ethanoate ion accepts protons from water, forming OH- ions
questions.explanation: CH3COO- + H2O <=> CH3COOH + OH-. Sodium ethanoate is the salt of a weak acid and a strong base.

questions.stem: In terms of electron transfer, oxidation is
questions.explanation: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

questions.stem: In terms of electron transfer, reduction is
questions.explanation: The species that is reduced gains electrons, and its oxidation number falls.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of manganese in KMnO4?
What is the oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7?
questions.explanation: 2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(-2) = 0, so 2Cr = +12 and Cr = +6. Answering +12 forgets that there are two chromium atoms.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in sodium thiosulphate, Na2S2O3?
What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in the ammonium ion, NH4+?
In the reaction 2FeCl2 + Cl2 -> 2FeCl3, chlorine acts as
questions.explanation: Chlorine takes electrons from Fe2+ (Fe2+ -> Fe3+) and is itself reduced to Cl-.

questions.stem: In the reaction CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, the substance that is reduced is
questions.explanation: CuO loses oxygen (Cu goes from +2 to 0), so it is reduced. Hydrogen is the reducing agent.

questions.stem: Which of these reactions is NOT a redox reaction?
questions.explanation: In neutralisation no element changes its oxidation number. Each of the others involves electron transfer.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of Fe2O3?
questions.explanation: 2Fe + 3(-2) = 0, so each Fe is +3.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of KClO3?
questions.explanation: There are three oxygens (trioxo), and Cl is +5 because +1 + Cl - 6 = 0.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of NaNO2?
questions.explanation: There are two oxygens (dioxo), and N is +3 because +1 + N - 4 = 0.

questions.stem: A gas decolourises purple acidified potassium tetraoxomanganate(VII) solution. This shows that the gas is
questions.explanation: MnO4- (purple) is reduced to almost colourless Mn2+, so the gas must have given it electrons.

questions.stem: Acidified potassium heptaoxodichromate(VI) changes from orange to green when
options: it is reduced by a reducing agent such as sulphur(IV) oxide
questions.explanation: Orange Cr2O7 2- (Cr +6) is reduced to green Cr3+.

questions.stem: Given MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O and Fe2+ -> Fe3+ + e-, how many moles of Fe2+ are oxidised by 1 mole of MnO4-?
questions.explanation: One MnO4- accepts 5 electrons and each Fe2+ gives up 1 electron, so 5 mol of Fe2+ are needed.

questions.stem: In the reaction H2S + Cl2 -> 2HCl + S, hydrogen sulphide is
questions.explanation: Removal of hydrogen is oxidation, and sulphur goes from -2 to 0.

questions.stem: In the reaction 2H2S + SO2 -> 3S + 2H2O, which substance is the oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: Sulphur in SO2 goes from +4 to 0, so SO2 is reduced and is the oxidising agent. H2S (S: -2 to 0) is the reducing agent.

questions.stem: Which of these substances is a non-electrolyte?
questions.explanation: Sugar dissolves as molecules, not ions, so its solution does not conduct electricity.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid using platinum electrodes, what is produced at each electrode?
options: Oxygen at the cathode and hydrogen at the anode
Sulphur(IV) oxide at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode
Hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
questions.explanation: H+ is discharged at the cathode. At the anode, OH- (from water) is discharged in preference to SO4 2-, giving oxygen.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of acidified water, what is the ratio of the volume of hydrogen to the volume of oxygen produced?
questions.explanation: 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2 and 4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e-. The same charge gives 2 mol of H2 for every 1 mol of O2.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution using copper electrodes, what happens at the anode?
options: Copper atoms dissolve to form Cu2+ ions
questions.explanation: A copper anode is oxidised (Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-). Copper is deposited at the cathode, and the solution keeps its blue colour.

questions.stem: When copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution is electrolysed using platinum electrodes, the solution
options: loses its blue colour and becomes acidic
questions.explanation: Cu2+ ions are removed at the cathode and oxygen is given off at the anode, leaving H+ and SO4 2- ions (tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid) behind.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine) using a carbon anode, the gas given off at the anode is
questions.explanation: Because Cl- is present at high concentration, it is discharged in preference to OH-.

questions.stem: What is formed at the cathode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed?
questions.explanation: In the melt the only cations are Na+, which gain electrons to form sodium.

questions.stem: When a very dilute solution of sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes, the main product at the anode is
questions.explanation: At low chloride concentration, OH- ions from water are discharged in preference, giving oxygen.

questions.stem: What mass of copper is deposited when a current of 0.50 A is passed through copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution for 1930 s? (Cu = 63.5; F = 96 500 C mol^-1)
questions.explanation: Q = 0.50 x 1930 = 965 C = 0.010 mol of electrons. Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, so 0.0050 mol of Cu = 0.318 g.

questions.stem: How much electricity is needed to deposit 5.4 g of silver from a solution of silver ions, Ag+? (Ag = 108; F = 96 500 C mol^-1)
questions.explanation: 5.4/108 = 0.050 mol of Ag, which needs 0.050 mol of electrons. 0.050 x 96 500 = 4825 C.

questions.stem: The same quantity of electricity is passed through two cells in series. One deposits 0.27 g of aluminium from Al3+ ions. What mass of copper is deposited from Cu2+ ions in the other cell? (Al = 27, Cu = 63.5)
questions.explanation: 0.27/27 = 0.010 mol of Al, which needs 0.030 mol of electrons. 0.030 mol of electrons deposit 0.015 mol of Cu = 0.953 g.

questions.stem: How long will it take a current of 2.0 A to deposit 1.30 g of zinc from Zn2+ ions? (Zn = 65; F = 96 500 C mol^-1)
questions.explanation: 1.30/65 = 0.020 mol of Zn, which needs 0.040 mol of electrons = 3860 C. t = 3860/2.0 = 1930 s.

questions.stem: What volume of oxygen, measured at s.t.p., is given off when 0.40 faraday of electricity is passed through dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid? (Molar volume at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm^3)
questions.explanation: 4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e-, so 4 faradays give 1 mol of O2. 0.40 F gives 0.10 mol of O2 = 2.24 dm^3.

questions.stem: Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the mass of a substance liberated at an electrode is
options: directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed
independent of the time of electrolysis
proportional to the volume of electrolyte
questions.explanation: m is proportional to Q, where Q = It.

questions.stem: In the purification of copper by electrolysis, the impure copper is made the
questions.explanation: The impure anode dissolves, and pure copper is deposited on a thin pure-copper cathode. The impurities fall as anode sludge.

questions.stem: Which of these metals will NOT liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the electrochemical series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from acids.

questions.stem: The standard electrode potentials are: Zn2+/Zn = -0.76 V and Cu2+/Cu = +0.34 V. What is the e.m.f. of the cell made from these two half-cells?
questions.explanation: E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode) = +0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V.

questions.stem: Galvanised (zinc-coated) iron still does not rust where the coating is scratched because
options: zinc is more reactive than iron and corrodes in preference to it
zinc is less reactive than iron
zinc forms an alloy with the iron
the scratch fills with zinc oxide, which is a reducing agent
questions.explanation: This is sacrificial (cathodic) protection: the more reactive zinc gives up electrons instead of the iron.

questions.stem: In a Daniell cell (zinc and copper half-cells), electrons flow through the external circuit
questions.explanation: Zinc is oxidised at the negative electrode, and its electrons travel through the wire to the copper electrode, where Cu2+ is reduced.

questions.stem: For iron to rust, it must be in contact with
questions.explanation: Rusting is an electrochemical process that needs both water and oxygen. Salt speeds it up.

questions.stem: For an exothermic reaction, the enthalpy change, dH, is
options: always greater than the activation energy
questions.explanation: Heat is given out to the surroundings, so the products have less enthalpy than the reactants.

questions.stem: When ammonium chloride dissolves in water, the beaker feels cold. The process is
questions.explanation: Heat is taken in from the surroundings, so dH is positive.

questions.stem: When sodium hydroxide pellets dissolve in water, the temperature of the solution rises. This dissolution is
options: a physical change with no heat change
questions.explanation: The heat released (mainly from hydrating the ions) raises the temperature, so the process is exothermic.

questions.stem: C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g), dH = -394 kJ mol^-1. How much heat is released when 6.0 g of carbon is burnt completely? (C = 12)
The standard enthalpies of formation are: CO2(g) = -394 kJ mol^-1, H2O(l) = -286 kJ mol^-1 and CH4(g) = -75 kJ mol^-1. What is the enthalpy of combustion of methane? CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O
questions.explanation: dH = [-394 + 2(-286)] - (-75) = -966 + 75 = -891 kJ mol^-1. -605 forgets the 2 moles of water, and -1041 gets the sign of the methane term wrong.

questions.stem: In which of these processes does entropy (disorder) increase?
options: A gas being compressed into a smaller volume
A solid salt dissolving in water
questions.explanation: When a salt dissolves, ions held in an ordered lattice spread through the solution, so disorder increases. The other changes increase order.

questions.stem: A reaction is spontaneous (feasible) when its free energy change, dG, is
questions.explanation: dG < 0 means the reaction is spontaneous, dG > 0 means it is not, and dG = 0 means the system is at equilibrium.

questions.stem: For a reaction, dH = +40 kJ mol^-1 and dS = +0.16 kJ mol^-1 K^-1. Using dG = dH - TdS, what is dG at 300 K, and is the reaction spontaneous?
questions.explanation: dG = 40 - (300 x 0.16) = 40 - 48 = -8 kJ mol^-1. A negative dG means the reaction is spontaneous.

questions.stem: When dG = 0 for a reaction, the system
questions.explanation: At equilibrium there is no net tendency for the reaction to go either forwards or backwards.

questions.stem: The enthalpy of neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is about
questions.explanation: The reaction in every case is H+ + OH- -> H2O, which releases about 57 kJ per mole of water formed.

questions.stem: 50 cm^3 of 1.0 mol dm^-3 HCl was mixed with 50 cm^3 of 1.0 mol dm^-3 NaOH, and the temperature rose by 6.8 °C. Taking the specific heat capacity of the solution as 4.2 J g^-1 K^-1 and its density as 1.0 g cm^-3, what is the enthalpy of neutralisation?
The breaking of chemical bonds is
questions.explanation: Energy must be supplied to break a bond. Energy is released when bonds form.

questions.stem: Potassium reacts vigorously with water, and the hydrogen produced may catch fire. This shows that the reaction is
questions.explanation: Enough heat is released to melt the potassium and ignite the hydrogen.

questions.stem: Powdered marble reacts faster with dilute hydrochloric acid than lumps of marble of the same mass because the powder
options: has a larger surface area exposed to the acid
questions.explanation: More surface means more collisions between the acid particles and the marble per second.

questions.stem: Raising the temperature increases the rate of a reaction mainly because
options: a larger fraction of the colliding particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy
the concentration of the reactants increases
more products are formed at equilibrium
questions.explanation: Particles move faster and collide more often, but the main effect is that many more collisions now have enough energy to react.

questions.stem: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by
options: providing an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
increasing the kinetic energy of the particles
shifting the equilibrium to the right
questions.explanation: With a lower energy barrier, more collisions are successful at the same temperature.

questions.stem: In the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, manganese(IV) oxide is added. The manganese(IV) oxide acts as
options: a reducing agent that is used up
questions.explanation: MnO2 speeds up 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2 and is left chemically unchanged at the end.

questions.stem: In the reaction between sodium thiosulphate solution and dilute hydrochloric acid, the rate is usually followed by
options: measuring the volume of hydrogen given off
weighing the flask to find the loss of oxygen
timing how long the precipitate of sulphur takes to hide a cross drawn under the flask
measuring the change in colour from blue to colourless
questions.explanation: Na2S2O3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + SO2 + S + H2O. The yellow sulphur slowly makes the mixture cloudy.

questions.stem: In a graph of the volume of CO2 given off against time for marble reacting with acid, the curve eventually levels off because
options: one of the reactants has been used up
the catalyst has been used up
the temperature has fallen to zero
questions.explanation: Once the limiting reactant is finished, no more gas is produced.

questions.stem: Magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Which change would NOT affect the initial rate of the reaction?
options: Using a larger volume of acid of the same concentration
Cutting the magnesium into smaller pieces
questions.explanation: The rate depends on concentration, not on the total volume. Extra acid of the same concentration does not change how often particles collide.

questions.stem: Increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction increases its rate because
options: the particles are closer together and collide more often
questions.explanation: For gases, a higher pressure has the same effect as a higher concentration.

questions.stem: A catalyst does NOT change
options: the enthalpy change of the reaction
the time taken to reach equilibrium
questions.explanation: dH depends only on the energies of the reactants and products, which a catalyst does not alter.

questions.stem: Suppose the rate of a reaction doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature. How many times faster is the reaction at 50 °C than at 20 °C?
questions.explanation: A 30 °C rise is three 10-degree steps, so the rate increases by 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times.

questions.stem: Enzymes are best described as
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins that speed up particular reactions in living things.

questions.stem: In a reaction, 40 cm^3 of gas was collected in the first 20 seconds. What was the average rate of gas production over this time?
questions.explanation: Average rate = volume/time = 40/20 = 2.0 cm^3 s^-1.

questions.stem: The iodine clock reaction is commonly used to study the effect of
options: light on the rate of reaction
surface area on the enthalpy change
concentration on the rate of reaction
questions.explanation: Changing the starting concentrations changes how long the blue-black colour takes to appear.

questions.stem: Food keeps longer in a refrigerator because
options: the low temperature slows down the reactions that cause spoilage
questions.explanation: Chemical and enzyme-controlled reactions are much slower at low temperatures.

questions.stem: Activation energy is
options: the energy released when a reaction takes place
the total energy of the products
the minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react
questions.explanation: Only collisions with at least this energy lead to a reaction.

questions.stem: A reaction is in dynamic equilibrium when
options: the forward and backward reactions take place at the same rate
all the reactants have changed into products
the concentrations of reactants and products are equal
questions.explanation: At equilibrium both reactions continue, but at equal rates, so the concentrations stay constant (though not necessarily equal).

questions.stem: For the equilibrium N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g), the forward reaction is endothermic. What happens when the temperature is raised?
options: More N2O4 forms, and the mixture becomes paler
More NO2 forms, and the mixture becomes darker brown
The position of equilibrium does not change
questions.explanation: By Le Chatelier's principle, the system takes in the extra heat by favouring the endothermic (forward) reaction.

questions.stem: For the equilibrium N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g), what happens when the pressure is increased?
options: The equilibrium shifts to the right, favouring NO2
The equilibrium shifts to the left, favouring N2O4
There is no change, because both are gases
questions.explanation: Increased pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules: 1 mole of N2O4 compared with 2 moles of NO2.

questions.stem: For the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g), dH = -92 kJ mol^-1, the yield of ammonia at equilibrium is increased by
questions.explanation: There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so high pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right. A high temperature would favour the backward (endothermic) reaction.

questions.stem: Adding a catalyst to a reaction mixture at equilibrium
options: shifts the equilibrium to the right
shifts the equilibrium to the left
does not change the position of equilibrium, although equilibrium is reached faster
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally.

questions.stem: Which is the equilibrium constant expression for H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)?
questions.explanation: Kc is the product of the product concentrations over the product of the reactant concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient.

questions.stem: Steam is passed continuously over heated iron in an open tube: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) <=> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g). The reaction goes almost to completion because
options: the hydrogen formed is swept away, so equilibrium is never set up
